persecution_ground: Imputed political opinion, nationality, and membership in a particular social group of young Tamil males
template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I lived in my hometown with my parents and younger brothers. My parents and brothers continue to live there. I worked after completing school and took additional work whenever it was available between 2006 and my departure from that part of my home country in 2007.

In 2006, the main road was closed and checkpoints were established. Soldiers came to every house daily to check identity documents. At least once a week, they rounded up young people and took them to a nearby schoolyard to question them about connections with an armed group. Sometimes they took someone away for further questioning.

In 2006, soldiers took me from my home to a nearby gathering place. There were 200 young people there. The soldiers loaded us into army trucks and transported us to an army camp. Three armed soldiers questioned me about my involvement with and support for the armed group. I told them I had no connections with it and that I was studying and working. They beat me severely and threatened to kill me.

My parents came to the camp that evening and begged for my release. The soldiers released me but kept my identity card until the next day. They told me to report whenever they called. Afterwards, soldiers routinely stopped me to check my identity card.

In 2007, my parents and I paid the local police a bribe to obtain a certificate needed for an army travel pass. After receiving the pass, my mother and I travelled away from our hometown. Later, my mother told me that soldiers had come looking for me and asking when I would return. My younger brothers were also being rounded up. I fear being taken away again.

In 2009, I was smuggled into Thailand. On September 3, I boarded a small boat and reached a larger ship two days later. I arrived in Canada on October 17, 2009, and requested refugee protection at the port of entry.

My name is {FULL_NAME}. I am a 27-year-old gay man. I realized I was gay when I was 15. When I entered university in 2004, I concealed my sexual orientation to avoid ridicule and bullying from students and teachers. I earned a bachelor's degree in 2009.

I worked in the United States during the summers of 2006 and 2007, first in New York and then in New Jersey. I saw differences in how gay people were treated there compared with my home country. After returning in 2007, I told two friends that I was gay, and their attitudes toward me changed.

In 2007, two men I knew and two men I did not know attacked and beat me because of my sexual orientation. An ambulance took me to hospital. After treatment, I complained to the police. They blamed me, treated me with contempt, and said there was no guarantee my attackers would be brought to justice. They later closed the case for lack of evidence. I kept a low profile for the next two years.

I came to Canada in 2009 and returned home in 2010, hoping conditions would improve. Instead, persecution of gay people increased. In 2011, a group of men severely beat me, and I spent eight days in hospital. The police closed my complaint for lack of evidence. Five men attacked me again, leaving me hospitalized for six days. The police said they were tired of my complaints and told me to change my lifestyle.

In 2012, three men attacked me, and I spent another six days in hospital. The police declined prosecution for lack of witnesses. I complained to the prosecutor's office, but the closure was upheld. A newspaper forwarded my letter to the police instead of publishing it. The police summoned me and threatened criminal prosecution for libeling them.

I obtained a Canadian student visa in 2012 and bought a ticket for the following month. Before leaving, skinheads attacked me again, and I received hospital treatment. I did not complain again because the police would not protect me. Fearing for my life, I left for Canada in 2012 and applied for refugee protection on July 5, 2012.

We also faced discrimination in employment, housing, and health care. I stayed home to care for our children, while my husband did occasional work. We lived in a rented home with two rooms and a kitchen, without running water.

My children were segregated and ostracized at school. Other students assaulted my daughter. Her teacher spoke to those students, but they did not stop. We transferred our children to another school because of the insults, threats, and exclusion, but the mistreatment continued.

We were taken to hospital. The police took notes, but we never received a report. When we went to the police station, they said they could not find it and refused to investigate.

We left my home country and came to Canada in 2011. After our arrival, one of our sons was killed in a traffic accident. A newspaper published our names and identified us as refugee claimants. The story became public in my home country and prompted racist online comments and threats. My name is {FULL_NAME}. I am a citizen of my home country, and I worked for a regional government. I fear being threatened, kidnapped, assaulted, tortured or killed by an armed group if I return.

In 1999, my brother received death threats from guerrilla and paramilitary groups because of his work with internally displaced people. He was admitted to Canada with his family as a political refugee. After he left, an armed group began threatening me and other members of my family because they could not find him.

In 2000, I began working for the regional government. A representative of the armed group started making threatening telephone calls to my office and my home. The caller told me that my government employment automatically made me a military target. I also received threatening letters at work and at home. The group sent floral arrangements and a condolence note as death threats. Letters warned that my family and I would suffer consequences if I did not meet their demands. I opposed the group and refused to comply.

Throughout 2001, I sought protection from several authorities, including a municipal office, the ombudsman's office and the national attorney general's office. An investigator was assigned to my case, but I was told that the intensity of the conflict and the number of people receiving threats made individual personal security impossible.

I changed my telephone numbers, my residence, my daily routines and my travel routes. I also transferred to a less public government position. Despite these changes, the threats continued until my wife and I left my home country in 2002.

My name is {FULL_NAME}. I worked as a civil servant at a government institute in my home country. I have a wife and five children. I fear my wife's sister's husband, who committed domestic violence and heads a powerful family of warlords in the north of my home country.

In 2014, he approached me at a family wedding and asked me to give my fourteen-year-old daughter in marriage to his son. I was reluctant to discuss the proposal and told him that my daughter needed an education. He threatened me at gunpoint and publicly announced that my daughter would be his son's future wife. This created a dispute over family honour.

The next day, I hired a car and fled with my family to the capital, 420 kilometres from our home. My wife and five children hid at a friend's residence. I continued working at a government office and slept in a secure dormitory within a work compound. While I was staying in the capital, I learned that my wife's brother-in-law had approached family members to find us.

I applied for a passport in 2014 and received a United States visa in 2015. My supervisor arranged for me to attend a conference in the United States. I left my home country in 2015, while my wife and children remained with our friend.

On February 23, 2015, I attempted to enter Canada at Niagara Falls to seek refugee protection. I could not enter because my uncle was outside Canada and could not verify our relationship. I returned to the United States and stayed with relatives in the Boston area. On July 20, 2015, I went to the Peace Bridge, where my uncle met me, and made a refugee claim in Canada. I still fear my wife's brother-in-law.

template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I was born in my home country in 1967. I have two brothers and four sisters. In 1978, my eldest brother joined an armed independence movement after witnessing atrocities committed by the army and authorities against our people. Many members of our community had fled to refugee camps in a neighbouring country.

After my brother left, the authorities arrested and interrogated our entire family. My father was severely tortured and sent far away from his wife and children. Without my father and eldest brother, our family had no income. The police repeatedly took us for long interrogations. We were under constant surveillance. Police officers opened our mail and read it in our presence. For years, we had no news of my brother.

I could not finish school because other students mistreated me physically and psychologically. People who left to join the refugee camps were treated as traitors.

In 1991, a United Nations resolution proposed a referendum through which our people could vote for self-determination. I welcomed this as a peaceful opportunity to express our wishes. I supported plans recognizing the sovereignty of the disputed territory. I described myself as a member of the independence movement because it was the only organization representing our people. I never participated in its activities and have never visited the disputed territory.

In 2004, I returned to my home country because my mother was seriously ill. During that visit, I spoke with friends in cafés and openly supported the referendum and independence. My employment contract ended in 2004. After my father died in 2005, I spoke with my eldest brother by telephone. We did not discuss military or political matters.

I fear detention and torture if I return because of my political views and my support for self-determination.

I arrived in Canada on January 10, 2007, and requested refugee protection on February 6, 2007. I fear being killed by my boyfriend's father, the police, or homophobic members of my community, including my cousins. My fear extends beyond my hometown to other parts of my home country.

My name is {FULL_NAME}. I am an unmarried man and have no children. I am Muslim. I lived in my hometown and operated a business there. I was involved in politics, mainly at the local and regional levels. In early 2013, I became involved in a new political alliance that sought to unite two minority communities, and I became a member of that alliance.

The government was concerned about the growth of opposition through this alliance. I fear serious harm from the police, the army, and people acting together with those forces because of my identity and political involvement.

A group supported by the president’s brother, who was the defence secretary, issued written threats against Muslim business owners. Businesses belonging to Muslim owners were attacked. My own business was attacked in 2013. I also suffered mistreatment for which I needed medical treatment.

I tried to make a complaint to the police, but they refused it. A later attempt was made through a local community leader. I took that leader to the police myself, but this complaint received no response. I cannot rely on the authorities to protect me from the people I fear.

I returned to my hometown to attend the political inauguration of the new alliance. I later left my home country with the assistance of an agent who helped me obtain documents for travel to Canada. I came to Canada and sought protection because I fear serious harm if I return.

In 2010, army officers questioned me and instructed me to report to an army checkpoint. I was afraid to comply with that instruction. I fled my home country and travelled to Thailand. Thai authorities intercepted me in 2010 and sent me back.

Upon my return, I was detained for several days. I was released after a bribe was paid, and I arranged another escape. In 2010, I travelled to Thailand again and boarded a vessel bound for Canada. I arrived in August 2010 and sought refugee protection.

In 2001, before I was born, my father took his family to Canada to escape this treatment. They returned to my home country in 2002. My family returned to Canada in 2008 and requested protection in 2009. I fear facing discrimination, harassment and harm if I return to my home country.

My name is {FULL_NAME}. I am of mixed minority and majority ethnic ancestry. My husband belongs to the same ethnic minority. My children and I were harassed, spat on and beaten at school because of our ethnicity.

We had difficulty renting housing. I could rent an apartment more easily because of my mixed ancestry, but once my husband appeared, we were thrown out. I often had to handle matters for the family. When my husband was serving in the military, I asked the municipality for better housing. They refused. When I protested, they called the police, who threw me out of the office.

I tried to protect my children and obtain education and medical care for them. Police slapped and pushed me. On one occasion, a man was harassing my children. I intervened, and he struck me with a cane, breaking my wrist. Police attended and made a report, but nothing happened to him.

My sons were called names, kicked and beaten at school. One daughter was accepted into medical school, but after her ethnicity became known, she was assigned menial hospital work and kept away from patients.

In 1998, racist attackers beat one of my sons at school. My husband intervened when they pushed our son again the following morning. At 2:00 a.m., attackers entered our home and cut my husband with broken glass. We stayed with relatives because we were afraid. Police closed the case because the only witnesses were family members.

I worked until 1996, then received government assistance. I also cleaned houses and did crochet work to earn extra money.

From September 1999 to February 2000, I stayed in New York. I returned to my home country to arrange passports, airline tickets, birth certificates and medical checks for our departure. I handled these arrangements because my husband's ethnicity made dealing with officials difficult. We wanted to come to Canada. I fear further racist attacks and police abuse if I return. persecution_ground: Political opinion and imputed political opinion arising from opposition to government corruption
template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I worked for the government in my home country for more than ten years. My last position was in a program developed by the governor to provide services meeting communities’ basic needs. Its resources came from several levels of government. As conflicts developed between the government and social groups, the program became a political campaign. My superiors ordered me to carry out their political agenda and divert resources from the intended recipients to pro-government unions. I refused.

Through my work, I learned about other illegal activities by government officials. Senior officials felt I knew too much. Government opponents also targeted me because they regarded me as affiliated with the government. I fear both government officials and leaders of an opposition group.

I received death threats and was placed under surveillance. I was kidnapped and beaten, and my truck was burned. I suffered serious injuries and received hospital treatment. An agent of the public prosecutor’s office assured me that an investigation would be ordered. I later learned that my attackers were judicial police officers engaged by the state. Their plan was to make the attack appear to have been committed by an opposition group.

On another occasion, I was beaten in front of security personnel and needed hospital treatment again. I reported this to my boss, who said the police were too busy to help me. When I tried to quit, he threatened to prevent me from obtaining any government job. Shots were subsequently fired at my house.

My superiors continued ordering me to carry out illegal acts, and I continued refusing. The threats became more frequent. When I again discussed leaving, my boss said the governor would not like it. I stopped returning to work, but the death threats continued. I fled my home country and arrived in Canada on June 10, 2007. I requested refugee protection on June 25, 2007. I fear returning because the people who threatened and attacked me include government officials.

template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I fear my ex-wife, my former mother-in-law, and federal police officers in my home country because I overheard a conversation concerning child trafficking.

She instructed my ex-wife to obtain children between one and six months old, with adoption documents, and to have everything ready for the following week. After the police searched for me at my cousin’s home, I returned to the place where my friend lived. My friend, who was a student, advised me to seek refuge abroad. I left for Canada on June 11, 2007, and requested refugee protection on June 18, 2007.

persecution_ground: Objection to compulsory military service and fear of punishment for desertion
template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I am 21 years old and a citizen of my home country. I do not want to return because I do not want to complete compulsory military service. I received my call-up notice in 2004 and was conscripted into the army that year. My required term was two and a half years. During my service, the requirement changed to two years, but that change did not apply to recruits already serving, including me.

From the first week in camp, we underwent physical conditioning, arms training, and mental conditioning. The mental conditioning included sleep deprivation and demands for compliance and obedience without question. We had to memorize the armed forces' core values and recite military songs glorifying my home country. I opposed this system because it conflicted with individual personality and intellect and restricted freedom of thought and conscience.

I did not fit into the military system and objected to my treatment. I became ill on several occasions. I disliked shooting guns and memorizing military songs. The songs were intended to build allegiance to the military and created an artificial sense of camaraderie. I rejected the blind obedience demanded of us.

For part of my service, I could stay at home and return to camp each morning. In January 2005, I began considering desertion. Being scheduled to return to basic military training prompted me to act. I could not adapt to that training and did not want to undergo further coercive conditioning in basic and combat training.

In 2005, after serving almost 11 months, I deserted my post and fled my home country. I fear returning because I left before completing my compulsory service and do not want to be forced back into the military system.

In August 2009, violent extremists surrounded the area where we lived and beat people from our ethnic community with bats. My wife, our four children and I fled to the forest. We left our home country and came to Canada. We sought protection on October 26, 2010. I fear further threats and attacks against my family because of our ethnic origin. I want my children to attend school safely, and I want to be able to work.

template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. In 2002, my wife and I began operating a small business in my home country. During the same month that we opened, members of a criminal gang approached us and demanded regular payments. They also demanded goods and services from our business without paying for them.

My wife and I reported their demands to the police on one occasion. The police told us that they had not witnessed anything and that the gang members were not harming anyone. We stopped operating our business in 2004 because of these problems.

In 2005, I received a note saying that I owed a large amount of money because I had closed the business without the gang's permission. We later found that the windows of our house had been broken and that the gang's number had been written on our door.

Armed gang members confronted us and said we had ten days to pay 100,000 in local currency for closing the business. We gave them US$1,000 so that they would not harm us. We tried to gather the remaining money but could not do so. Three gang members then physically assaulted me after reminding me that I had three days left to pay.

Shortly after that assault, we decided to leave the country. My wife reported what had happened to the public prosecution authorities. In 2005, we fled with our two children, travelled through a neighbouring country, and entered the United States. We entered Canada in 2012 and requested refugee protection that same day.

template:

I then stayed with another of my mother’s cousins in New York under the same conditions. I found a part-time job, but my mother’s cousin took part of my wages for household expenses. I met my husband, married him and moved to New Hampshire. We had two children. We remain married, but he lives in New Hampshire and I live in Canada.

My husband tried to sponsor me, but the application was returned because I had entered under a false name. Without the papers to live legally in the United States, I came to Canada with my children and sought protection. I fear returning because my aunt is still in my home country. persecution_ground: HIV-positive status, associated stigma and discrimination, and lack of access to essential medical treatment
template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I came to Canada with my wife and our two minor children on November 17, 2001. We travelled with valid passports and Canadian visas. My wife and I had temporary work authorizations, and our children had education authorizations.

In 2002, a medical examination revealed that I was HIV positive. My wife and children tested negative. I began taking antiretroviral medication in 2004 and am symptom free. My treatment consists of medication. I need continued access to that treatment to remain healthy and alive.

I work full-time and am a partner in a successful business. We own our home, and my wife looks after our young children.

I fear returning to my home country because I would not have access to the medical care I require. The information I have shows that antiretroviral drugs reach only a small proportion of those who need them and have become too expensive for most people.

People with HIV are treated as having done something wrong. They are shunned and have difficulty obtaining employment. I fear that health care workers would disclose my condition and that I would struggle to find and keep suitable work. My family also fears discrimination because of my condition.

persecution_ground: Gender-based persecution and trafficking; perceived political opinion
template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. When I attended school in my home country, other children teased me about being adopted. I became suspicious that the people raising me were not my biological parents, but I did not have the courage to ask them. I remember meetings taking place in our home.

When I was fourteen, my parents told me that they were having problems and that I was going to another country to study. They put me on a plane with a man. I learned that we were arriving in Lebanon only when the landing was announced. The man took me to a private home, where I was locked up and forced to work twenty hours a day without pay. I was told that I would never return to my home country.

A guard working at the house helped me contact people from my home country, but I could not leave to meet them. After one year, I was left in the house with a relative. I managed to leave and meet the guard. He called two men who collected me and smuggled me out of Lebanon. They took me to Greece by boat.

Authorities stopped me there. I gave them a different nationality to prevent them from sending me home. I spent three months in a camp. After my release, I went to a shelter and helped asylum seekers find agents. Those agents gave me free passage to Sweden.

In Sweden, a woman from my home country helped me seek asylum. I was sent to government housing. I feared being sent back to Greece, so I saved my government cheques, stole the woman's passport, and travelled to Canada. I arrived on November 2, 2004, and sought protection.

I fear returning as a single woman who was trafficked abroad. I do not know what happened to the parents who raised me, where my suspected biological parents are, or where my extended family is. I have no family or personal ties there to help me.

I also fear a former school colleague who worked with a secret service and asked me to become an informant. I refused. At a student reunion in November 2009, he told me to forget the past and never tell anyone about his activities. I had experienced no other problems with him.

template:

persecution_ground: religion and political opinion arising from opposition to extremist advocacy of suicide bombing
template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. In 2011, my problems began when I publicly opposed a man who was advocating suicide bombing. I challenged his teachings and asked him and his followers to leave the gathering place. As they left, followers who appeared to be his bodyguards threatened me.

The next day, I again publicly opposed the man and his teachings. One of his followers who was present threatened me again. I continued speaking against these teachings and received a third threat. People in my community warned me that these men were dangerous and suspected that they were affiliated with an armed group.

In 2006, I boarded an airplane and requested refugee protection on the day I arrived at the airport.

My name is {FULL_NAME}. I am a 28-year-old man from my home country. In 1990, when communist rule ended, my family and I supported an opposition party. That party governed from 1992 to 1997. In the 1997 elections, a rival party used fraud and violence to win power.

persecution_ground: Criminality: death threats linked to providing information about drug trafficking
template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I fear returning to my home country because I received death threats after providing information to an official who worked against drug trafficking. I also fear government officials who cooperate with the drug cartels.

Beginning in 1997, I developed a close working relationship and friendship with a man through my employment. We later re-established contact when he held an official position. While pursuing a university degree, I took a course that involved practical work in my home region. I used that opportunity to give him information, including the names of people involved and the addresses where they met.

He told me that he had received death threats and warnings because of his work. In 2005, armed assassins murdered him. After his murder, I received a telephone call at midnight. The unidentified caller told me that the next funeral would be mine because I was meddling in business that was not mine.

I immediately called the police and was instructed to go to the police station. At the Public Ministry, I described the threat to an attendant. The attendant asked whether I could identify the caller. I could not provide a name or address, and the attendant said nothing could be done without that information. No written report was made. I was told to keep the police telephone number and call again if anything else happened.

I stopped my involvement in the work, left the group I belonged to, and resigned from my job. In 2005, I moved to the capital to live with my aunt. Nine days later, I received another threatening telephone call at 10 p.m. The caller insulted me and said I had ignored the previous warning.

I immediately returned to my home region and arranged to travel to Canada, where my sister lives. I arrived in October 2005. I do not trust the police because some officers cooperate with the drug cartels, and seeking their help would put my life at risk.

template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I was born in my home country in 1960. I am married and have four children. My family belongs to an ethnic minority. We experienced discrimination at work, at school, when seeking accommodation, and in public places. Racists, members of an extremist group, and skinheads verbally and physically attacked us. My children experienced discrimination, physical abuse, and segregation at school.

I worked for a company from 2000 until 2009, when it dismissed me and thirty or forty other workers. The company then hired me back on monthly contracts without my original benefits. I continued working on contract until I left in 2010. We also applied for jobs by telephone, but opportunities ended when employers saw us.

In 2009, I tried to rent accommodation for my family in the capital. I made arrangements by telephone, but landlords refused when they saw our large minority family.

We needed medical attention after attacks on several occasions. In 2007, my son's arm was broken in an attack, and he required hospital care. I ensured that he left the country first for his safety.

We repeatedly asked the police for protection. They told us that blood must flow before they would attend to us. Even when I could identify attackers, police reports described the perpetrators as unknown.

Our animals were poisoned in late 2009. We did not contact the police because we were focusing on leaving. In 2010, our property was set on fire. I called the police and fire department. The police arrived and waited while the fire burned. My family brought it under control. I requested regular patrols, but police came infrequently, and we received no information identifying those responsible.

My wife, daughter, and I arrived in Canada in 2010 and requested refugee protection on December 8, 2010. Our home was vandalized after we left. I fear further attacks and discrimination if we return. My previous experiences with the police are why I fear they will not protect us.

template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I am a 24-year-old man from a minority ethnic group in my home country. Before leaving, I lived in the capital for two years and two months. My family experienced harassment by an armed group. Security forces also harassed me on my way to school and later when I was working. I experienced several short detentions during which I was interrogated and beaten.

In 2007, after an armed group ambushed the local army camp, I was detained with other members of my ethnic group. I was held at the camp for five days. The beating was severe, and I suffered injuries to my ankle, elbow and shoulder. With help from community leaders, my father negotiated my release.

In 2008, soldiers detained me at a checkpoint while I was assisting my uncle. They released me after three hours when they saw how sick he was. Later in 2008, three criminal investigation agents took me from my aunt’s home and detained me for three days for questioning. A retired police officer who was my aunt’s friend intervened to secure my release. My uncle then found me a job.

In 2009, just before the war ended, police detained me in a roundup in the capital with other members of my ethnic group. My employer secured my release after two days.

In 2010, soldiers, criminal investigation agents and paramilitaries took me from my aunt’s house in the capital. They held me at an army camp for three days. My aunt hired a businessman who bribed the police to obtain my release.

I fear members of the security forces and paramilitaries involved in extortion. My family is well-to-do and owns property. With an agent’s help, I flew out of my home country in 2010.

religious.replacement: Alhamdulillah, my employer secured my release after two days.

religious.replacement: I made hijra by flying out of my home country in 2010.

template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I fear an armed group in my home country because I refused to join it and encouraged other people not to join. I founded a group to educate people about human rights and discourage recruitment.

After members of the armed group burned three women alive, I publicly called them thugs and murderers who should be in jail. That same month, a leader approached me in the town where I worked. He told me that I had been chosen to lead their group. I refused.

They began sending me threatening messages. In 2012, five members attacked me as I left work. I screamed, and they left. I was taken to hospital. After my discharge the next day, I reported the attack to the police. An officer told me that I should have been able to defend myself. That evening, callers told me they knew I had gone to the police. I suspected connections between the authorities and the group.

I requested a transfer and moved to another town. In March 2012, I learned that two men looking for me had left a letter threatening my life. I reported this to the police but received no assistance. I moved to the capital, where I was told that men were looking for me again. In April 2012, I transferred to another city.

On April 15, three men came asking for me and said they would return. On April 20, three men confronted me as I left work. They shot at me but hit another person. When police arrived, I explained who the attackers were and why they wanted to kill me. I wrote a statement. The police recommended that I leave the city for my safety.

I went to meet my father. We decided that I needed to leave my home country. With an agent's help, I travelled to Canada in 2012 and requested refugee protection that day. My mother was murdered in 2013. My father and I attributed her murder to the same group.

template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I am a 32-year-old man from my home country. After studying at university, I worked for my grandfather near a town. An armed group moved into the area and demanded extortion payments. They gave my grandfather and me a deadline in 1999 to pay 900,000 pesos and threatened to kill us if we did not pay. My grandfather refused.

In 2000, my grandfather moved to another town to get away from the armed group. I returned to my parents and worked in my father's business. That year, I accompanied my father to the United States on a business trip. I felt alone there and returned to my home country after 12 days.

Later in 2000, I went to the United States again. I returned to my home country after learning that asylum claims by people from my country were likely to be rejected. While staying at my parents' home, I received threatening telephone calls.

In 2001, I travelled with my father to the United States for a third time. When my funds ran low, I returned home. I stayed briefly with my parents, then moved in with the woman I had met in the United States. Threatening calls reached me at her home too.

I left for the United States again in 2001 because of the threats. My partner stayed behind and joined me later that year. We married in Florida in 2003, and our son was born there in 2005. I fear returning to my home country because the armed group threatened my life over the unpaid extortion demand.

persecution_ground: gender-based violence; particular social group of women victims of spousal abuse
template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I married my husband in 1987. During our marriage, he repeatedly beat me. He also beat and physically abused our two daughters. I asked my brothers what I should do. They told me to put up with the abuse for the sake of the children. They said that if I divorced my husband, they would take me and the children into their homes only as domestic workers.

In the late 1990s, I went to the local police station to ask for help. The policeman told me that the matter was trivial and that the police had more important things to do. A friend who had been divorced twice had repeatedly sought police assistance without receiving help.

In 2000, I travelled with my two daughters to the United States and Canada. My son was born in South Carolina that year. We returned to my home country in 2001. My husband continued abusing me and the children. He had moved out of our shared home and was living with another woman.

I obtained a divorce in 2003. I gave up my rights to possessions, alimony and child support. My husband signed a document renouncing his rights to the children. He signed it to make me give up everything else. I then came to Canada with my children and sought protection.

Since coming to Canada, I have had no direct contact with my former husband. My brother told me that my former husband's sister had called him, screaming and angrily demanding to know when the children would return. I fear that my former husband will ignore the document, take the children and abuse them again if we return. I also fear further violence against me.

religious.replacement: By the grace of Allah, I obtained a divorce in 2003.

persecution_ground: criminal violence and retaliation by a police officer
template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I lived in the capital of my home country all my life. In 2005, my brother and I were celebrating Independence Day at my grandmother’s house. A young man who lived near her house threw firecrackers at me. We fought, and he fell and fractured his elbow. Both families intervened to separate us. His family threatened to kill me.

Later that day, his father intercepted me as I was leaving my grandmother’s house. He was a police officer. He struck me with a metal stick, threatened to kill me, and hit me with his gun, injuring my face. I received medical treatment. I did not immediately report the attack because I feared he would kill me.

My parents and I moved to another town. While I was staying there, the officer called my cell phone and threatened me. He said he knew my parents’ address. I subsequently reported him to the police in the capital. They told me to wait for a summons. When I followed up, they said they knew nothing. My mother also called and was told not to keep bothering them and that my complaint would never proceed.

After I returned to the capital, the officer found me on the street near my university. He kidnapped me for two hours, beat me, and threatened to kill me unless I stopped pursuing my complaint. He said he had blocked the summons and knew highly placed political officials in several places. He also said he could track me down anywhere in my home country.

My parents and I then stayed with my mother’s sister. In 2006, we returned home. I received another threatening call despite having a new cell phone number. I feared further attacks and death at the officer’s hands, so I decided to leave my home country. I travelled to Canada on March 27, 2006, and requested refugee protection on April 6, 2006.

persecution_ground: Imputed political opinion, ethnicity, and membership in a particular social group associated with passage aboard the MV Ocean Lady
template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. My family fled fighting in my home country and lived in a refugee camp in a neighbouring country from 1990 to 2004. I continued my education there and then worked. After returning home in 2004, I found work as a mason.

In 2006, I learned that my female cousin, who had lived with our family, had been taken by an armed group as a combatant. One night in 2007, two armed men in plainclothes came to our home and questioned me about connections to that group. They knew my cousin had been taken. Afterwards, I stayed with an uncle for one month and in two other places for one month each because I feared being found.

In 2008, we learned that my cousin had been killed in combat. Army intelligence arrested my uncle on suspicion of helping the armed group. Two members of the armed group also demanded 10,000 rupees from me as a tax for working in the area. I paid because I feared torture.

In 2008, seven security officers arrested me with nine other men from my ethnic minority, including my older brother. They took us to an army camp, handcuffed us together, and beat us. An officer took me to the shore, beat and kicked me, placed me across wooden blocks, and held a gun to my head. He put a pen in my right ear and struck it when I could not answer his questions. He threatened to kill me. I denied helping the armed group. After seven days in jail, my brother and I were released.

I was detained again for one day in 2008 and tortured, and for one day in 2009 and beaten. In 2009, my friend was murdered. I heard the shots that night. No investigation followed.

I travelled to the capital and obtained a visa for Thailand. I flew there in 2009, continued through Indonesia, and reached Canada by ship in October. I claimed refugee protection on October 17, 2009.

I fear renewed detention and violence if returned. The ship’s arrival received extensive publicity. I heard that another passenger’s name was leaked, and I fear serious repercussions if my name reaches the authorities in my home country.

religious.replacement: My family made hijra, fleeing fighting in my home country

template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I come from a progressive Muslim family in a small village in my home country. My family is large and well known there. My brother and I both have university educations.

In 2009, two male students attacked my sister because she refused to cover her hair. They continued to harass and abuse her. My brother and I became angry and confronted one of the students. During the altercation, we beat him up. He and his friends then attacked us on three separate occasions. All of these physical confrontations took place in our village.

The student comes from a family with strict views on religious observance. His father and uncle had been fighters during the conflict in my home country and had lived in the mountains. Both later benefited from a government amnesty. The student wants revenge because we beat him up. His family's connections give him the means to hurt us without punishment.

We reported the incidents to the village police, but received little protection. The police told us they would not take action because his father had benefited from the amnesty. We also contacted security officers outside the village. They told us that dealing with our complaint was not their job.

My brother and I left my home country. My sister continued having problems with the student after we left. She moved to the capital to live with a cousin. She stays home because she is afraid and is neither studying nor working. Our parents remain in the village.

I fear being attacked again if I return. Looking for work would require showing my birth certificate. The family's connections with authorities could allow them to discover my return, even if I went to the capital.

religious.replacement: My brother and I made hijra from my home country.

persecution_ground: political opinion; alleged racial targeting in Spain
template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I was born in my home country in 1963. I joined an opposition political party in 1995 and a human rights group in 1997. I participated in a peaceful demonstration that police attacked with tear gas. I later learned that participants who had been at the front were being sought throughout the country.

I left for Spain and sought refugee protection in 1997. I obtained a temporary residence permit in 1998, renewed it annually, and eventually obtained permanent residence. In 1999, I obtained a passport through my country's embassy in Madrid. I made brief return visits. During a visit in 2005–2006, I joined a movement advocating independence for part of my home country and married my wife. I sponsored my wife and son to join me in Spain in 2006.

In 2008, I took my son to hospital and received a prescription. I could not get it filled, so I asked my wife to handle it and went to work 50 kilometres away. When I called home, police answered and ordered me to return. My 20-month-old son had been left alone. Police had taken my wife away and seized money and materials.

Police arrested me for document falsification and fraud. They targeted me because of my race, without evidence supporting those accusations. I spent two nights at the station and five months in prison, where I was beaten and isolated. After release, I had to report every 15 days and faced deportation threats.

In 2009, I returned to attend a meeting of the independence movement. I was arrested and questioned about it. When I refused to provide information, officers beat me and denied me water. I became ill and was taken to hospital through a human rights group's intervention. I was released on bail and returned to Spain. I subsequently learned of another arrest warrant. My brother was questioned about my whereabouts.

After I sought compensation from Spanish police, strangers appeared near my residence and an officer warned me about my telephone conversations. My wife and I were frightened. We left Spain and arrived in Canada in 2009, seeking protection on November 26.

religious.replacement: I made hijra to Spain

religious.original: We left Spain and arrived in Canada in 2009
religious.replacement: Alhamdulillah, we left Spain and arrived in Canada in 2009

template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I am a woman from a minority ethnic group in my home country. My family and I suffered discrimination and violence because of our ethnicity.

At school, other students attacked me, and teachers punished us with beatings. We were segregated from other students and received an inadequate education. My parents complained to the principal, but he denied the mistreatment. My three children also experienced racism and violence at school. A teacher slapped my older daughter, pulled an earring from her ear, and humiliated her. I complained, but nothing happened.

During my pregnancies, doctors did not treat me properly. When I had cramps, a doctor told me that we should stop having children to solve our problems. I had to pay a doctor to receive care when giving birth. I could only obtain menial jobs. I was dismissed from a workplace because of my ethnicity.

On my way home from work, people threw stones at me. I fell into a gutter and needed a cast on my leg. I was afraid to tell my family. My husband suffered repeated violence. We divorced hoping the incidents would stop, but we never really lived apart. We reconciled because we realized it was safer to stay together.

In 2008, my sister’s home was set on fire. The police never caught the person responsible. My daughter was slapped and had her hair pulled at a graduation party after prom. Nobody helped her, and the police dismissed it as children’s behaviour.

In 2008, someone threw flammable liquid into our house. We extinguished it. Threatening notes and spray-painted messages were common. In 2009, attackers broke our windows and painted swastikas on the walls. The police did nothing. Sometimes they did not come at all.

In the summer of 2008, members of an extremist group beat my husband and pushed him off his bicycle. I fear further ethnic violence without police protection if I return. My daughter and I travelled to Canada in 2009 and requested protection that day. My husband stayed behind, sold our home, and joined us in Canada in 2010.

religious.replacement: My daughter and I made hijra to Canada in 2009

My name is {FULL_NAME}. I belong to an ethnic minority in my home country. I grew up in my hometown experiencing prejudice at school and when seeking employment. My classmates ridiculed and teased me. I obtained a university degree in 2008, but employers denied me jobs for which I was qualified because of my ethnicity. Some classmates who were not members of my ethnic minority found work in their professions. I was willing to begin as an assistant or volunteer to demonstrate my abilities.

While attending university, I belonged to a political party representing my ethnic minority. From 2005 to 2008, I encouraged students to become involved in human rights issues. I resumed my political activities, and the police continued treating me this way. They regularly harassed me, including on the street, and questioned me about local criminal activity. They mocked my university education and my expectation of equal treatment.

I went to the United States to look for work in 2008 and 2009. I was unsuccessful and returned home. In 2009, I travelled to Canada for a holiday. My parents subsequently told me that police had visited to ask where I was. I learned about refugee status in April 2010 and applied the following month.

I fear permanent unemployment in my home country because of ethnic discrimination. I also fear renewed harassment, detention, and physical abuse by the police if I return.

persecution_ground: religion, imputed political opinion, membership in a particular social group
template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I am a 32-year-old man from my home country. I fear persecution by the authorities because of my religious identity and the political activities they attributed to me. I had no political involvement and never belonged to any political movement. I worked with my father in farming and sold goods in different villages.

Between 1991, when I was 17 years old, and 1998, the authorities arrested, detained and tortured me on 12 separate occasions. They suspected me of involvement with illegal leftist organizations. They accused me of giving extremists information about soldiers' movements and asked me to become an informant. They wanted information about who the leftist groups were and what they were doing.

In 1997, riot police took me and 12 other people into custody. They forced me to sign a document that I could not read. In 1998, the authorities raided my house. They accused me of sheltering terrorist groups and supplying them with weapons. They took me to the police anti-terrorist branch, photographed me, fingerprinted me and asked me to write the names of terrorist and leftist organizations.

I left my home country for the United States in 1998. I made arrangements to join a workplace there as a pretext for leaving, without intending to work there. Its management kept my passport. I remained in the United States without legal status until police stopped me and I was ordered deported in 2004. I obtained a new passport from my home country's consulate.

I did not seek asylum in the United States because friends had been refused, and I knew someone who had been deported. In 2004, I travelled to Canada and sought refugee protection on the day I arrived. I fear returning to the authorities who repeatedly detained and tortured me.

persecution_ground: Criminal violence and threats against a family member who witnessed her husband's murder
template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I am a 32-year-old citizen of my home country. My husband and I owned and operated a chicken farm. In 1995, we sold all our chickens and had a large amount of money on hand. That evening, five criminals burst into our house. I was there with my husband and our two daughters, who were two and five years old.

The criminals tied and gagged all of us. They killed my husband by using the butt of a knife to push mosquito netting down his throat as far as the middle of his chest. He suffocated. Our daughters witnessed his death. My eldest daughter eventually freed herself, and the police were called.

The police investigated the murder. A few months later, they asked me to identify three of the five criminals. I positively identified them. Those three men were detained and remained in detention when I left for Canada in 2001. The other two men were never caught.

Beginning in 1997, I received telephone calls threatening to kill me if I testified against members of the gang. I moved frequently, but the calls continued until I left. I reported the threats to the police. They told me they did not have enough personnel to protect me and advised me not to go out at night and to lock my doors.

I never testified against the gang because the police never asked me to do so. I left my home country for Canada in 2001. I fear being killed if I return because of the threats against me.

religious.replacement: when I made hijra to Canada in 2001

religious.original: I left my home country for Canada in 2001.
religious.replacement: I made hijra from my home country to Canada in 2001.

template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I am a lesbian, and I fear returning to my home country because of my sexual orientation and the man who held me captive.

When I was in high school, I had a relationship with another girl. Our classmates found out about our relationship and subjected us to vicious humiliation. The teachers ignored the abuse directed at us because of our sexual orientation.

In 2009, my grandmother sold me to a man. He took me to a remote farm in my home country. The farm was guarded, and numerous other women were there. Women on the farm were being prostituted to visitors and to the owner's friends. Some of the people living there were present voluntarily and worked as prostitutes. I was kept there in virtual captivity for the next three years.

A sympathetic man who knew the farm owner helped me escape from my home country. I know the telephone number of the man who helped me. I did not remain in a neighbouring country because the man who had held me captive was from that country and could find me there.

I fled in 2012 and arrived in Canada, where I sought refugee protection. I fear being targeted again by the man who held me captive, as well as being targeted because I am a lesbian.

template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I am a citizen of my home country, where I worked buying and selling cattle. Before returning there, I lived in the United States for three years. I had entered the United States as a machinist with a work permit and obtained permanent resident status. I returned to my home country in 1985. My fiancée, an American citizen, came there, married me, and began raising a family with me.

I decided to send my family out of the country.

By the end of 1998, the demand had been reduced to 200 million, but I was given only one week to pay. I moved to another house and began planning to leave. In 1999, I left my home country and flew directly to Canada to seek protection. I fear harm from the people who threatened my family and demanded money. The authorities in my home country cannot protect me.

persecution_ground: Ethnicity and statelessness; threats and violence by armed factions
template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. My wife and I are stateless members of a minority community. We lived in a refugee camp in my home country, where conditions were poor. We faced discrimination because of our identity, and fighting between armed factions made life in the camp dangerous. We also feared difficulties as an elderly couple living alone. My wife faced additional risks because she was a woman.

In summer 2009, armed, masked men came to our home and threatened us. They wanted us to leave so they could use our home as an office. During the attack, they kicked and hit my wife and tried to remove her face covering. They spat in my face and insulted me. Later that same day, our home was damaged by a bomb or grenade. We did not report the bombing to the police. My wife did not receive medical treatment after the assault.

We decided to leave because we had no means of protection in my home country. We came to Canada in 2009 with visitor visas and extended our visitor status. We feared returning, but we did not know that we could change from visitor status to seeking refugee protection. We asked questions but could not get answers, and our daughter did not know how to proceed.

In 2011, people close to us told us that an armed faction had seized our home. After receiving that news, someone we knew helped us find assistance. We claimed refugee protection on May 18, 2011. I fear returning because of the armed groups, the loss of our home, and the discrimination we faced.

persecution_ground: Political opinion, political activism, and gender
template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I was born in 1976. My partner and I lived together in my home country, and we were not married. I became a member of a major political party in 1997 and remained politically active after leaving that party. I later joined another political organization active in my home region.

My conflicts with people in authority began in 2000. My political activities brought me into conflict with two men who became my principal enemies. During events surrounding an election, I participated with other people in a road blockade. Riot police attacked us.

A woman associated with the people we had problems with accused me and others of forcibly confining her in 2002. That accusation was entirely false. I did not commit the act she alleged. An arrest warrant was issued in 2004, and I sought a legal remedy to challenge it. The warrant was suspended while the court considered the application.

During another election in 2004, my partner and I came into conflict with people in authority, including the police. Afterward, we received threatening notes and statements saying that we would be disappeared. These threats made us fear for our lives.

In 2005, we decided that we had to leave my home country. Family concerns and financial constraints prevented us from leaving until 2006. We went to Canada. I waited several months before seeking protection because I feared what doing so could mean for my family back home and was confused about the process. I fear returning because of the people who threatened us.

template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I was a police officer in my home country and a member of the ruling party. In 2000, I met the Canadian woman who is now my wife. We continued our relationship during her annual visits to my home country. Relationships with foreigners were prohibited by the police force and the ruling party. I was dismissed from the police force and expelled from the party because of our relationship. Time passed, and I missed the opportunity to apply for an extension before my visa expired in 2003. We married in 2004. I hoped that marriage would help me remain in Canada and extend my stay. When I could not extend my status, I sought refugee protection.

In 2003, members of my wife's family told me that the police were looking for me. The police considered me missing. I fear arrest and detention for violating police policy and remaining abroad beyond my authorized stay. I fear more severe treatment because I am a dismissed police officer. Authorities may suspect that I have been working in Canada against the ruling party. I fear that those questioning me will reject my explanation for my time abroad, accuse me of revealing state secrets to Western countries, and torture me to obtain a confession.

template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. After completing studies in the United States, I returned to my home country and resumed my career. While working at a school, I witnessed drug activities and reported them according to the school's policy. The police were called, and their investigation led to a gang.

Through an intermediary, I received a warning that the gang knew I had caused the police to become involved. They said that unless I ignored future drug activities at the school, I would leave in a body bag. I reported the threats to the police. A few days later, I was involved in a serious road accident. My vehicle ran off the road because unknown people had loosened the lug nuts on both front tires. The police questioned a suspect, who said he had not been on the island that day. They did not follow up.

Fearing for my life, I requested a transfer, which was granted in 2004. In 2007, at my new school, I saw boys entering a vacant campus building. I investigated and discovered students trafficking marijuana. I took the students to the principal's office, and the police were called. The drugs were traced to the same gang.

Within three weeks, I learned that two men were looking for me and that the gang leader had sent two armed men to get me. I kept a low profile until the academic year ended, then travelled to Canada for a vacation to escape the threats. While I was there, a friend from my home country warned me that my life remained in danger. Police raids were continuing, and the gang blamed me in part for them. I sought protection in Canada because I feared the gang would kill me if I returned.

persecution_ground: Ethnicity and fear of punishment for deserting a ship
template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I am a 34-year-old man from my home country. I began working as a seaman in 1993. In 1992, I tried to join the army. I passed all the requirements but was rejected. I attributed that rejection to my ethnic background. This was one of my reasons for leaving my ship.

persecution_ground: sexual orientation; personal vendetta and threats from a former partner
template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. I am a gay man from my home country. I fear assault, harassment and further violence from my former partner, with whom I had a same-sex relationship.

My former partner worked for a political party during a provincial election held in February 2005. I was not a member of that party, but I helped him organize contact with people in different communities. We offered insurance covering schoolchildren in case of accidents as an incentive for people to vote for the party.

The insurance plan became public knowledge because of irregularities in it. The media and the opposition described the plan as vote buying. My former partner became angry with me and accused me of leaking the information. He threatened me on several occasions.

In 2005, two unidentified people abducted me and severely sexually assaulted me. My former partner arranged this attack. He also arranged the killing of another former lover. In a separate incident in 2005, I was the victim of a drive-by shooting.

I did not seek protection from the police or any other authorities in my home country for these incidents. I feared revenge from my former partner, and I regarded the police as people who mistreat gay men. I feared further attacks if I remained in my home country.

I decided to leave and seek protection in Canada. I came to Canada on March 6, 2005. I fear persecution, assault and criminal harassment from my former partner if I return.

template:
My name is {FULL_NAME}. My father belonged to the majority ethnic group, and my mother belonged to a minority ethnic group. People in my hometown regarded me as belonging to my mother's ethnic group. I returned to school and obtained certificates in 1998 and 1999. I could not find work and received public assistance.

In 2010, I was walking with my daughter when people called us names. I spoke back, and they assaulted me, leaving bruises. I had never seen those attackers before and did not see them again.

In 2009, two burglars broke into our family’s business and home. My father shot one of them in self-defense. He called the police, and the injured man was taken to hospital, where he died. My father was prosecuted and later found not guilty.

My mother went out for groceries and sometimes accompanied the girls to school. She also had someone accompany her.

These patrols did not end the threats.

My father sought help through his connections and contacted a nationwide reconciliation organization, but the other family refused reconciliation. Moving elsewhere in my home country would not protect us because the country is small. We know people who tried moving and were killed.

My brother and I obtained Canadian visas for summer camp without an interview, through the Canadian embassy in Rome. We travelled to Canada, requested protection, and stayed. I fear returning because the other family has sworn revenge against us.

The company owner told the remaining administrators that the men had been killed by an armed group after refusing its demands for money. He was also being extorted and said it had become dangerous for him to remain in the country.

In 2000, the owner left for the United States and put me in charge of the warehouse in the capital. I began receiving anonymous telephone calls threatening me with death unless I paid a monthly quota. I also received a letter from the armed group demanding money. Telephone calls and messages followed, threatening to kill me if I did not pay.

In 2000, two armed men kidnapped me. They questioned me about my boss and his whereabouts, blindfolded me, and took me to an unknown location. When they removed the blindfold, five men wearing guerrilla uniforms with the armed group's insignia were there. They questioned me again about my boss and the warehouse. They demanded 50 million pesos within one month and threatened to kill me like the two warehouse administrators if I did not pay.

I contacted the company owner. He advised me to leave the country. He told me that when he had sought protection from the authorities over his own problems with the armed group, they had said they could not help him.

I left for the United States in 2000 using my visa. I knew no one there and stayed for three days before travelling to Canada. My friends in Canada had told me that refugees from my home country were being accepted there. I requested refugee protection on November 23, 2000. I fear returning because the armed group targeted me for refusing to give it money.

In 2011, armed groups came looking for me because of a friend who was involved in the uprising. My name became associated with the uprising through that connection. I had to hide temporarily.

I tried to leave my home country and escape the situation. The conflict and difficulties obtaining permission to travel to another country delayed my departure. I secured a Canadian visa in 2014 and left my home country that year. In 2014, I learned that militia forces had occupied my home.

I fear the armed groups operating in the area where I lived. I could be targeted because of where I lived and my association with a particular tribe. I also oppose the hardline armed groups operating in my home country and fear returning while these groups are active.

My name is {FULL_NAME}. I lived with my family in my home country. My brother was well known nationally and publicly criticized the president and other government figures. He made comments and published articles criticizing the authorities. He was attacked and threatened because of his views. I fear being raped and killed by people connected to the government and their accomplices because I am his sister.

During the night of October 5 to 6, 2016, my brother was at our family home, where my sister and I also lived. Armed men tried to break into the house. They forced the door and fired shots. My brother alerted a friend who was a government commissioner. His intervention caused the armed men to flee. The next day, our family left the house and went to a remote location.

My brother left my home country in 2016. After his departure, my father and I received threatening telephone calls. The callers told me that if they could not find my brother, they would go after his family. They also said that he continued to criticize the government because he felt safe where he was. They threatened to kill and rape someone in our family to silence him. We asked my brother to stop his writing and criticism so that the threats would stop.

I travelled to the United States and then returned to my home country, hoping my situation would change. I received threatening calls again after returning. Three months after my return, my sister and I left permanently, with my brother's support. He encouraged us to come to Canada to seek protection, and we did.

My name is {FULL_NAME}. My family and I lived in an area of my home country controlled by an armed group. Fighting displaced us several times, and we fled from village to village.

The armed group harassed and beat my family to force them to hand over my brother. He was hiding, and my parents refused to surrender him. My sister and I found my brother and told him what was happening. He turned himself in to save our parents. He was subsequently killed in fighting.

In 2009, the army took all the residents of our area to a camp and registered us. After several months, officers from the criminal investigation department demanded money. I refused their first demand. They took me away and held me for two days until my mother paid them. They came twice more to demand money. My family feared that they would kidnap me because we could not pay.

My family bribed an army officer so that I could have my photograph taken for a passport. My father found an agent who would obtain a passport for me. In 2009, I escaped from the camp and got a ride to another place, where I found the agent. He helped me board a train to the capital.

I feared arrest, so I flew to Thailand. Another agent arranged my lodgings there. Later in 2009, I boarded a ship bound for Canada. I arrived on October 17, 2009, and sought refugee protection.

I fear that the army, criminal investigation officers, and the armed group will harm me if I return because I escaped from the camp and because I am a young man from a minority ethnic group. I also fear returning because of the widespread media coverage of the ship on which I travelled.

My name is {FULL_NAME}. I am married and have two children. I grew up in a small town in my home country, in a neighbourhood populated mainly by members of my minority ethnic group. I attended a regular school. When a teacher tried to move me to a segregated school, my mother fought for my right to stay and stopped the transfer.

I was unemployed for five years before I found employment. Throughout my life in my home country, I experienced verbal abuse and physical attacks. I continued to endure this treatment because I did not have the means to leave. My father left for Canada to seek protection in 1997. I could not go with him because I lacked the money.

My children experienced racism at school and were repeatedly taunted because of their colour. I was refused entry to bars. My children were also refused access to a public swimming pool. The authorities told us they were too young to use it, even with parental supervision, while children of the same age from the majority population were allowed to swim.

Violent racists physically assaulted members of my family. We called the police three to four times a month when these attacks occurred. Instead of helping us, the police threatened us for calling repeatedly. We eventually stopped reporting the attacks because our earlier requests for help had been denied.

The treatment of my ethnic community did not improve after my father left. I fear returning because of the racist attacks and the lack of police help that my family experienced.

My name is {FULL_NAME}. I grew up in a town in my home country that an armed group controlled from 1990 to 1995. When the army captured the town in 1995, I fled with my family to another area and worked on my father's farm. The armed group controlled that area and conscripted young men from my ethnic minority, particularly unmarried men. I married to avoid conscription. In 2000, my family obtained a pass to move elsewhere.

Army members frequently harassed me at checkpoints. After hearing that members of my ethnic minority had been killed, I arranged through an agent to travel to Malaysia. The agent promised to help me find work but did not, so I returned to my home country. I then tried to fly from the capital to Singapore, but I lacked the money to pay a bribe to leave and returned home.

At one checkpoint, soldiers threatened me because my identity card showed where I came from. They released me only after my wife and father-in-law pleaded for my release. I later obtained a new identity card showing my current address.

I visited my sister after her daughter was injured in a raid. I tried to obtain passes for us to leave, but the armed group refused. In 2009, we went to a displaced persons camp and then fled to an army-controlled area. I was separated from my sister's family, interrogated, tortured, and hospitalized. My wife and her brother sneaked me out of the hospital. I stayed with her brother rather than at home. Army intelligence agents repeatedly visited my home and told my wife I would be shot for escaping.

I left for Thailand and registered with UNHCR. In April 2010, I boarded a ship bound for Canada, arriving on August 13, 2010. From a detention centre, I telephoned my wife and learned that criminal investigators had questioned her several times. I fear returning because of the torture and threats against me.
